title: United States | Bank Cybersecurity: GLBA Safeguards, NYDFS Part 500 and Incident Notification
tagline: Protect customer information the way US bank regulators expect: GLBA safeguards, NYDFS Part 500, phishing defence and the 36- and 72-hour notices.
sectors: Foreign bank branches in New York
description:
This quest teaches the cybersecurity rules that US banks work under. At federal level it covers the **Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards** issued under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) by the OCC, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC, their guidance on response programs for unauthorized access to customer information, and the 2021 **computer-security incident notification rule** (the 36-hour rule). At state level it covers the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) cybersecurity regulation, **23 NYCRR Part 500**, as amended in 2023.

You will learn which duties apply to every federally supervised bank and which apply only to institutions licensed or chartered by NYDFS, and practise spotting phishing and social engineering, managing access, handling an incident against the 36- and 72-hour clocks, overseeing service providers and reporting to the board.

It is meant for all staff of US banks, and in particular staff of NYDFS-regulated banks and New York branches of foreign banks, where Part 500 requires cybersecurity awareness training, including social engineering, at least once a year. The federal guidelines require every bank to train staff to implement its information security program. This quest builds knowledge and does not replace your institution's own information security policies, incident response plan and training.
audience: All employees of US banks who handle customer information or use bank systems
Staff of NYDFS-regulated banks and New York branches and agencies of foreign banks
IT, security operations and incident response teams
Vendor managers and business owners of outsourced services
CISOs, senior managers and board members who oversee the security program
outcomes: Explain which cybersecurity duties apply to all federally supervised banks and which apply only to NYDFS covered entities
Describe the parts of a GLBA information security program, including staff training, testing and the annual board report
Recognise phishing, vishing, MFA fatigue and pretext calls, and respond and report the right way
Apply least privilege, access reviews, prompt removal of access and MFA to protect customer information
Classify an incident and meet the 36-hour federal notice, the NYDFS 72-hour notice and customer notice expectations
Support third-party oversight, CISO and board reporting and the NYDFS annual compliance filing

quest.name: The 36-Hour Clock
quest.premise: You have just joined the information security office of Kestrel Point Bank, a fictional New York-chartered bank that is a member of the Federal Reserve, with headquarters in Manhattan, an operations center in Buffalo and branches across the state. With CISO Priya Raman, incident lead Tomas Herrera, branch manager Grace Okafor, third-party risk head Kenji Mori and board risk chair Ellen Whitaker, clear five stages before the Federal Reserve and NYDFS examiners arrive, then face the final boss.

sessions.title: The Rulebook: GLBA Safeguards, NYDFS Part 500 and Who Must Comply
sessions.summary: Who sets US bank cybersecurity rules, what the federal GLBA information security guidelines require of every bank, and when NYDFS Part 500 adds a second, stricter layer.
objectives: Name the federal banking agencies and NYDFS and explain which banks each one supervises for cybersecurity
Describe the parts of a written information security program under the Interagency Guidelines
Explain who is a covered entity under 23 NYCRR Part 500 and what a limited exemption does and does not remove
Separate duties that apply to all federally supervised banks from duties that apply only to NYDFS-regulated institutions

cards.title: Day one: two examiners, one bank
cards.setting: Information security office, Kestrel Point Bank headquarters, Manhattan. 8:30 am.

lines.text: Your new laptop asks you to set up multi-factor authentication before it will even open email. A sticky note on the screen says: 'Welcome. Read the Rulebook first. Priya.'
Welcome aboard. I'm Priya Raman, the bank's CISO. Good news: you joined in exam season. The Federal Reserve and NYDFS are both coming to look at our cybersecurity.
Grace Okafor, branches. Why do we get two regulators? My cousin works at a national bank in Philadelphia and she only talks about the OCC.

Because we are a New York-chartered bank that is a member of the Fed. Federal rules apply to every bank with a federal supervisor. New York adds its own rule for the institutions it licenses or charters.
Kenji Mori, third-party risk. And our sister bank in Philadelphia is a national bank, so the OCC is its supervisor and Part 500 is not its rulebook.
Exactly. Stage one is the Rulebook Vault: who writes the rules, what every bank must do, and what New York adds. Let's open it.

scenes.heading: The federal layer
scenes.narration: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act told the banking agencies to set standards for protecting customer information. The OCC, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC answered with the Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards. Each agency publishes the same text for the banks it supervises.

scenes.heading: Who checks your bank
scenes.narration: Your primary federal regulator depends on your charter. National banks have the OCC. State banks that are members of the Federal Reserve have the Fed. State banks that are not members have the FDIC.

scenes.heading: The New York layer
scenes.narration: New York's Department of Financial Services wrote its own cybersecurity regulation, Part 500 of Title 23 of the New York codes. It applies to anyone operating under a New York banking, insurance or financial services license or charter.

scenes.heading: Both at once
scenes.narration: A New York-chartered bank like Kestrel Point must meet both layers. Where they differ, you follow the stricter or more specific duty, such as New York's yearly awareness training and its own 72-hour incident notice.

scenes.heading: Why training sits at the center
scenes.narration: Both layers name training. The federal guidelines tell every bank to train staff to carry out its security program. Part 500 requires awareness training, including social engineering, for all personnel at least once a year.

cards.question: Kestrel Point Bank is a New York-chartered bank and a member of the Federal Reserve. Which pair of regulators examines its cybersecurity?
options: The Federal Reserve and NYDFS
The OCC and NYDFS
The FDIC and the OCC
Only NYDFS, because the bank has a New York charter
cards.explanation: A state member bank's primary federal regulator is the Federal Reserve, and as a New York-chartered bank it is also a covered entity under Part 500. The OCC supervises national banks, and the FDIC supervises state banks that are not Fed members.

cards.title: What the federal guidelines require of every bank
cards.body:
The Interagency Guidelines apply to every bank supervised by the three agencies. Each bank must have a **comprehensive written information security program** with administrative, technical and physical safeguards that fit its size, complexity and activities. The program must be designed to:

- keep customer information **secure and confidential**
- protect against **anticipated threats** to that information
- prevent **unauthorized access or use** that could cause a customer substantial harm or inconvenience
- make sure customer and consumer information is **disposed of properly**

To build it, the bank **involves the board**, **assesses risk**, **manages and controls risk** (including training staff and testing key controls), **oversees service providers**, **adjusts** the program as things change and **reports to the board at least once a year**. Customer information covers records in any form, paper or electronic.

cards.title: The GLBA information security program cycle
cards.caption: Every federally supervised bank runs this loop; there is no finish line.

items.label: Board approves and oversees
items.detail: The board or a board committee approves the written program and assigns responsibility for it

items.label: Assess risk
items.detail: Identify foreseeable internal and external threats, their likelihood and damage, and whether controls are enough

items.label: Manage and control risk
items.detail: Choose controls, train staff, test key controls and dispose of information properly

items.label: Oversee service providers
items.detail: Due diligence, contract terms and monitoring where the risk assessment calls for it

items.label: Adjust the program
items.detail: Update for new technology, threats, outsourcing, mergers and system changes

items.label: Report to the board
items.detail: At least yearly: program status, compliance, tests, breaches and recommended changes

cards.title: Grace's question about the small branch
cards.setting: Video call between the Brooklyn branch office and the CISO's office.

lines.text: One of our customers runs a tiny New York-licensed money business with eight staff. She asked me if Part 500 applies to her. Does it?
If she operates under a DFS license, she is a covered entity. But Part 500 has a limited exemption for very small firms, based on staff numbers, revenue or assets.
So she can skip the whole thing?

No. The limited exemption removes some sections, such as the CISO and the incident response plan duties. It does not remove the yearly awareness training with social engineering, the risk assessment or multi-factor authentication for key access.
And she has to file a notice of exemption with DFS. An exemption is claimed, not assumed.

cards.title: The national bank colleague
cards.situation: Your colleague at the Philadelphia sister bank, a national bank supervised by the OCC, says: 'Part 500 does not apply to us, so we do not need any security awareness training at all.' Her team handles customer account data every day.

choices.text: Agree. Training is a New York requirement, so a national bank can skip it.
choices.outcome: This is wrong. The federal guidelines apply to national banks too, and they require the bank to train staff to implement its information security program. Skipping training would leave a gap the OCC can cite.

choices.text: Explain that the federal guidelines also require staff training, even though they set no yearly frequency, so her bank must still train staff under its own program.
choices.outcome: Right. The OCC's version of the Interagency Guidelines requires training to implement the program. Part 500's yearly social engineering course is the New York rule, but federal training is not optional.

choices.text: Tell her to follow Part 500 in full because New York rules apply to every US bank.
choices.outcome: Not quite. Part 500 applies to New York covered entities, not to every bank. Some banks choose to adopt it as a benchmark, but it is not her legal rulebook.

cards.question: A small DFS-licensed firm qualifies for the Part 500 limited exemption. Which duty still applies to it?
options: Designating a CISO who reports to the board in writing
Keeping a written incident response plan tested every year
Running endpoint detection and response tools
At least yearly cybersecurity awareness training that includes social engineering
cards.explanation: The limited exemption removes several sections, including the CISO duty, the incident response and continuity plan section and parts of 500.14, but not the awareness training in 500.14(a)(3). Endpoint detection is a Class A duty.

cards.title: Real case: Capital One and the OCC (2020)
cards.body:
In August 2020 the **OCC** fined two Capital One national banks **USD 80 million** and issued a separate cease-and-desist order. The OCC found that, around 2015, the bank had not set up effective **risk assessment** before moving its IT operations to the cloud, and lacked adequate network security controls, data loss prevention and handling of alerts.

Internal audit missed many of these gaps and did not report them clearly to the audit committee. Where audit did raise concerns, the **board did not hold management accountable**. The OCC found the bank out of compliance with its version of the **Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards**.

**Lesson:** the federal guidelines are enforceable. A risk assessment must come before a major technology change, and the board's oversight duty is tested by what it does with bad news.

cards.title: Real case: PayPal and NYDFS (2025)
cards.body:
In January 2025 **NYDFS** settled with PayPal, a DFS-licensed money transmitter, for **USD 2 million** under Part 500.

In 2022 an engineering team changed how tax forms were shown to customers. The team **had not been adequately trained** on the company's code deployment rules, so it misclassified the change and skipped the required risk review and testing. The forms went live showing full Social Security numbers. Criminals then used **credential stuffing** (trying stolen passwords in bulk) to reach those forms, and multi-factor authentication was **optional** for the affected customer accounts.

DFS found failures in policies and procedures, in qualified and trained cybersecurity personnel, and in access controls.

**Lesson:** training is a control. People who change systems must know the rules they are expected to follow.

cards.title: Stage one takeaways
items: Every bank with a federal supervisor must follow the Interagency Guidelines: a written, board-approved program built on risk assessment
The federal guidelines require the bank to train staff to implement the program but do not set a training frequency
Part 500 applies only to NYDFS covered entities, such as New York-chartered banks and DFS-licensed branches of foreign banks
Part 500 adds a CISO, yearly awareness training with social engineering, a 72-hour notice and an April 15 filing
A limited exemption removes some Part 500 sections but not the yearly awareness training

cards.prompt: Find out who your institution's primary federal regulator is and whether it is also a NYDFS covered entity. Which of the duties in this stage would change for you if the answer were different?

quiz.question: A state-chartered bank in Ohio is not a member of the Federal Reserve. Which agency is its primary federal regulator for the information security guidelines?
options: The OCC
NYDFS
The Federal Reserve
The FDIC
quiz.explanation: State non-member banks are supervised at federal level by the FDIC, which publishes its own copy of the Interagency Guidelines. The OCC supervises national banks and the Fed supervises state member banks.

quiz.question: Under the Interagency Guidelines, who must approve a bank's written information security program?
options: The head of IT, with the CISO's countersignature
The primary federal regulator before the program takes effect
The board of directors or an appropriate committee of the board
The bank's external auditor after its yearly review
quiz.explanation: The guidelines require the board or an appropriate board committee to approve the written program and oversee it. Regulators examine programs but do not pre-approve them.

quiz.question: Which statement about staff training under the federal Interagency Guidelines is accurate?
options: Training is recommended but is not mentioned in the guidelines
Only IT staff must be trained; other staff are out of scope
Banks must train all staff every quarter using a regulator-approved course
Banks must train staff to implement the program, but the guidelines set no frequency
quiz.explanation: Training staff to implement the information security program is one of the risk control duties in the guidelines. The text does not prescribe a frequency or a course; the bank decides based on its program and risks.

quiz.question: A London-headquartered bank operates a New York branch licensed by DFS. Its compliance head believes Part 500 does not apply because the parent has its own group security program. What is correct?
options: Only the parent bank is covered, so the branch needs no program of its own
Part 500 applies only to New York-chartered banks, not to branches
The branch is exempt because its parent is supervised in the United Kingdom
The branch is a covered entity, but it may adopt the parent's program if that program meets Part 500
quiz.explanation: DFS confirms that licensed New York branches of foreign banks are covered entities. Part 500 lets a covered entity adopt an affiliate's program, but the program must satisfy every applicable section.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the stated objectives of a bank's information security program under the federal guidelines?
options: Keeping the bank's marketing plans confidential from competitors
Ensuring the proper disposal of customer and consumer information
Maximising the return on the bank's IT budget
Guaranteeing that no security incident will ever occur
quiz.explanation: The four objectives are security and confidentiality, protection against anticipated threats, protection against harmful unauthorized access or use, and proper disposal. No program can promise zero incidents.

quiz.question: Kestrel Point's Philadelphia sister bank is a national bank. A manager there asks whether it must send DFS a yearly Part 500 compliance filing. What is the best answer?
options: No; it is not a New York covered entity, though federal guidelines still apply
No, because national banks are exempt from all cybersecurity rules
Yes, because any bank serving New York customers must file
Yes, because its holding company also owns a New York-chartered bank
quiz.explanation: Part 500 covers entities operating under New York licenses or charters. A national bank operates under an OCC charter, so the federal guidelines and the 36-hour rule apply, not the DFS filing.

quiz.question: A DFS-licensed firm with 12 employees believes it qualifies for the limited exemption. What must it do?
options: Nothing; small firms are automatically outside Part 500
Stop all cybersecurity training until it grows past 20 staff
File a notice of exemption with DFS and still meet the sections that remain
Ask the Federal Reserve to confirm the exemption in writing
quiz.explanation: A covered entity that qualifies for an exemption must file a notice of exemption with DFS within 30 days of the determination. The limited exemption removes some sections only; awareness training and other duties stay.

quiz.question: In the 2020 Capital One enforcement action, which governance failure did the OCC specifically highlight?
options: The board approved a cloud migration that the OCC had prohibited
The board appointed a CISO who lacked a US security clearance
The board did not hold management accountable for concerns raised by internal audit
The board failed to file a yearly certification with the OCC
quiz.explanation: The OCC found that internal audit missed many gaps and that, where audit raised concerns, the board did not take effective action to hold management accountable. There is no federal yearly certification like the DFS filing.

quiz.question: Which description of 'customer information' under the federal guidelines is correct?
options: Only data that includes a Social Security number
Records with nonpublic personal information about a customer, whether paper or electronic
Only electronic records stored in the core banking system
Any information the bank publishes about its products
quiz.explanation: The guidelines define customer information as any record containing nonpublic personal information about a customer, in paper, electronic or other form, kept by or for the bank.

quiz.question: In the 2025 PayPal settlement, why did NYDFS treat a training gap as a cybersecurity violation?
options: The CISO had not personally delivered the training sessions
The company trained staff on a framework that DFS had not approved
An untrained engineering team skipped the required risk review, exposing customer data
Staff had failed to complete the yearly phishing course on time
quiz.explanation: DFS found the engineers were not adequately trained on deployment policies, misclassified the change, skipped the risk review and testing, and exposed unmasked Social Security numbers. That broke the personnel and training duty and the policy duties.

sessions.title: Phishing, Vishing and Social Engineering
sessions.summary: Why both rulebooks focus on the human layer: recognising phishing, phone pretexts and MFA fatigue, reporting fast, and what Part 500's yearly social engineering training must cover.
objectives: Explain the federal training expectation on pretext calling and the Part 500 duty to include social engineering in yearly training
Recognise phishing, vishing, pretext calls, business email compromise and MFA fatigue attacks
Respond to and report a suspected social engineering attempt in the right order
Describe how banks measure whether awareness training works

cards.title: The help desk that wasn't
cards.setting: Brooklyn branch back office, 4:50 pm on a Friday.

lines.text: Priya, one of my tellers just got a call from 'IT support'. They said her VPN token was failing and asked her to log in on a page they texted her.
Did she do it?
She started to. Then the page asked her to approve a push on her phone and she stopped. Something felt off: our help desk never texts links.
Tomas here from Buffalo. Good instinct. That is the same playbook used against Twitter in 2020: a fake help desk call, a look-alike login page and a push approval.
She did the most important thing: she stopped and told someone. Grace, ask her to report it through the phishing button and the security hotline right now.
I will. But how do I train fifteen tellers to spot this every time?
That's this stage: the Lure Lagoon. Let's learn the lures.

scenes.heading: The lure
scenes.narration: Social engineering attacks the person, not the system. The attacker builds a story that makes you want to help: an urgent request, a fake problem, a familiar name or a reward.

scenes.heading: Many channels
scenes.narration: It arrives by email as phishing, by phone as vishing, by text as smishing, and in person. Attackers often combine channels, for example an email followed by a call that confirms it.

scenes.heading: What they want
scenes.narration: They want credentials, a multi-factor approval, a payment, customer data or a change to account details, such as a new phone number or payee.

scenes.heading: The pause
scenes.narration: Your best defence is a pause. Check the request through a channel you already trust, never through the contact details in the message itself.

scenes.heading: Report every time
scenes.narration: Report even when you did not fall for it. One report can reveal a campaign aimed at dozens of colleagues and lets the security team block it.

cards.title: From lure to loss: where you can break the chain
cards.caption: Every stage you stop earlier saves more. A report at the contact stage protects everyone.

items.label: Reconnaissance
items.detail: Attacker studies staff names, roles and habits from public sources

items.label: Contact
items.detail: Email, call or text with a believable story and urgency

items.label: Action
items.detail: Victim clicks, enters credentials or approves a push

items.label: Access
items.detail: Attacker enters systems and looks for data or payments

items.label: Loss
items.detail: Data theft, fraudulent payments or ransomware

cards.question: Which statement correctly compares the federal and New York training duties on social engineering?
options: Both rules require a quarterly phishing simulation for every employee
Part 500 expressly requires social engineering in yearly training; the federal guidance expects training on pretext calling and fraud schemes
Only the federal guidelines mention social engineering; Part 500 covers technical staff only
Neither rule mentions social engineering, so it is left to bank policy
cards.explanation: 23 NYCRR 500.14(a)(3) requires at least yearly awareness training that includes social engineering for all personnel. The Fed's small-entity guide to the federal guidelines says banks should train staff to recognise and respond to fraud schemes such as pretext calling.

cards.title: What Part 500 says about awareness training
cards.body:
Under **23 NYCRR 500.14(a)(3)**, every covered entity must provide **cybersecurity awareness training** that:

- is given **periodically, and at least once a year**
- reaches **all personnel**
- **includes social engineering**
- is **updated to reflect risks found in the entity's risk assessment**

This duty survives the limited exemption for small firms. Part 500 also asks for more targeted training: **cybersecurity personnel** need updates and training sufficient for the risks (500.10), and employees who carry out the **incident response and continuity plans** need training on their roles (500.16).

At federal level, the guidelines require every bank to **train staff to implement** its program. The Fed's compliance guide gives examples: teach staff to recognise and respond to **pretext calling** and other fraud or identity theft schemes, train IT staff in computer security, and train staff to dispose of customer information properly.

cards.title: Red flag or normal?
cards.prompt: A request lands in your inbox or phone. Sort each one.

items.text: A caller from 'IT' asks you to read out the code just sent to your phone
An email from the CFO's personal webmail asks for an urgent, secret wire before 5 pm
A vendor emails new bank details for its invoices and asks you not to call because the phones are down
A push approval appears on your phone when you are not logging in
The service desk replies to the ticket you opened, inside the ticketing system
Your manager asks you in a team meeting to finish this year's awareness course by month end
A 'customer' calls asking to change the account's phone number but cannot answer the security questions and grows angry
The security team announces a planned phishing test in the staff newsletter

cards.title: Real case: an MFA prompt approved four times (NYDFS, 2021)
cards.body:
In March 2021 **NYDFS** fined Residential Mortgage Services, a DFS-licensed mortgage banker, **USD 1.5 million**.

In March 2019 an employee who handled loan applicants' personal data clicked a link in a **phishing email** that appeared to come from a business partner, and entered her email password on a fake page. The firm used multi-factor authentication, so the password alone was not enough. But that evening she **approved the push prompt on her phone four times**, although she was not logging in herself. She reported it only after a fifth prompt the next day.

IT blocked access but did not check what data the mailbox held, so **no one notified consumers or DFS**. The event was first disclosed to DFS examiners about 18 months later.

**Lesson:** MFA helps only if staff know never to approve a prompt they did not start, and report it at once.

cards.title: Real case: the Twitter help desk calls (NYDFS report, 2020)
cards.body:
In October 2020 **NYDFS** published its investigation of the July 2020 Twitter hack, which hit accounts of several DFS-licensed cryptocurrency firms.

The attackers **phoned Twitter employees pretending to be the IT help desk**, offering to fix VPN problems that were common after the move to remote work. They sent staff to a **look-alike VPN login page**, captured the credentials in real time, and got some employees to **approve the MFA prompt**. With that access they took over high-profile accounts and posted a bitcoin scam, collecting over **USD 118,000**.

DFS noted the attack used no malware and no sophisticated exploits, just phone calls. It recommended stronger MFA such as hardware security keys, fewer people with access to powerful internal tools, and better staff training.

**Lesson:** a confident voice on the phone can beat expensive technology.

lines.text: An email arrives in the treasury mailbox, signed with the CFO's name. It asks for an urgent USD 480,000 wire to a new supplier account 'before the cut-off', and says the CFO is in a board meeting and cannot take calls.
The supplier is real, we use them. But the account number is new and the email says not to call.
Urgency, secrecy, a new account and a block on calling back. That is four red flags in one message.
If it is genuine and we miss the cut-off, the CFO will be furious.
A real CFO will forgive a ten-minute call-back. A fraudulent wire may never come back.

cards.title: What do you do with the wire request?
cards.situation: You are the treasury analyst handling the email above. The sender address looks right at a glance but is one letter different from the bank's domain. The supplier exists in the vendor master file with a different account number on record.

choices.text: Send the wire; the supplier is genuine and the CFO's name is on the email.
choices.outcome: This is how business email compromise succeeds. The look-alike domain and changed account details are classic signs. The money would likely be lost and the bank would have to report the fraud.

choices.text: Reply to the email asking the CFO to confirm the new account details.
choices.outcome: Better than paying, but you are asking the attacker to confirm their own story. Replies go to the fake address. Verification must use a channel you already trust.

choices.text: Hold the wire, verify with the CFO and the supplier using contact details already on file, and report the email to security through the phishing button.
choices.outcome: Right. Out-of-band verification using known contacts stops the fraud, and the report lets security block the domain and warn others. If it was genuine, the delay costs minutes, not money.

cards.title: Your five-step response to a suspected lure

items.label: Stop
items.detail: Do not click, reply, approve or pay; do not forward the message to colleagues

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Use a known channel: the number on file, the intranet directory or walking over

items.label: Report
items.detail: Use the phishing button or security hotline; give time, sender and what you did

items.label: Contain
items.detail: If you clicked or approved, say so at once so security can reset access

items.label: Learn
items.detail: Share the pattern in team briefings without blaming the person who reported

cards.title: Name the technique
cards.prompt: Match each attack to its description.

pairs.right: A fraudulent email that pushes you to click a link, open a file or enter credentials
A phone call from someone pretending to be IT, a regulator, a customer or an executive
A caller posing as a customer to get account details or change contact information
Repeated push prompts sent in the hope that you approve one to make them stop
Email from a real or spoofed executive or supplier account asking for a payment or bank detail change

cards.front: Myth: 'We have MFA, so phishing is no longer a risk.'
cards.back: Fact: attackers can trick people into approving prompts or entering codes on fake pages. MFA must be paired with training, and stronger methods resist this better.

cards.front: Myth: 'If I clicked a link, I should keep quiet to avoid trouble.'
cards.back: Fact: a fast report lets security reset access before damage spreads. Silence is what turns a click into a breach.

cards.front: Myth: 'Phishing tests are about catching people out.'
cards.back: Fact: tests measure whether training works and show where to focus it. Reporting rates matter as much as click rates.

cards.front: Myth: 'Training once at hiring is enough.'
cards.back: Fact: Part 500 requires at least yearly training for all personnel, updated for risks in the risk assessment.
Fact: phone, text, video and in-person pretexts are all social engineering, and Part 500 training must cover the topic.

cards.question: A teller receives six MFA push prompts in two minutes while she is serving a customer and not logging in. What should she do?
options: Deny the prompts and report them to security at once, because someone likely has her password
Approve one prompt so the alerts stop and she can keep working
Ignore them; prompts she did not start cannot cause harm
Turn off her phone until the end of the day and report it tomorrow
cards.explanation: Unexpected prompts mean someone is trying to log in with her credentials. Approving gives access, as in the Residential Mortgage case. Waiting delays the password reset that would shut the attacker out.

cards.title: Make your awareness training count
cards.body:
- **Tie it to the risk assessment**: Part 500 requires training to be updated for the risks the entity has identified, so last year's slides are not enough.
- **Cover every channel**: email, calls, texts, collaboration tools and in-person visitors.
- **Teach the report, not just the spot**: make the reporting route one click or one call.
- **Target high-risk roles**: payments, treasury, executive assistants, call centers and IT help desks.
- **Keep evidence**: completion records and content updates show examiners the duty was met.

cards.title: Stage two takeaways
items: Part 500 requires all personnel to receive cybersecurity awareness training with social engineering at least once a year
Federal guidance expects banks to train staff to recognise fraud schemes such as pretext calling
Never approve an MFA prompt you did not start, and never share a one-time code
Verify unusual requests through a channel you already trust, not the contact details in the message
Report every lure quickly, even if you clicked; a fast report is the strongest control

cards.prompt: Think of the last unusual request you received at work by email, phone or text. Which red flags did it show, and do you know exactly how to report one at your institution?

quiz.question: How often must a NYDFS covered entity give cybersecurity awareness training to its personnel under Part 500?
options: Periodically, and at least once a year
Every two years, aligned with the exam cycle
Only at hiring, with refreshers left to the CISO
Quarterly, with a mandatory phishing test each time
quiz.explanation: Section 500.14(a)(3) requires periodic, but at minimum annual, awareness training including social engineering for all personnel, updated for the risks found in the risk assessment.

quiz.question: Which content must Part 500 awareness training include?
options: Instructions for configuring firewalls
The bank's yearly financial results
A test on the text of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
Social engineering
quiz.explanation: Part 500 expressly requires that awareness training include social engineering and be updated to reflect risks the entity identified.

quiz.question: A caller claims to be an account holder, gives the correct name and address, and asks the call center to change the phone number on file because 'my phone was stolen'. The caller cannot answer the security questions. What is the best response?
options: Decline the change, follow the verification procedure and flag the call as a possible pretext
Change the number because the name and address match
Ask the caller for the full card number instead and proceed if it is right
Change the number and send a confirmation code to the new phone
quiz.explanation: Changing contact details is a classic step in account takeover. Name and address are easy to find; failing verification is a red flag. The federal guidance expects staff to be trained to resist pretext calling.

quiz.question: In the Residential Mortgage Services case (NYDFS, 2021), what allowed the attacker into the employee's mailbox despite multi-factor authentication?
options: A vendor shared its administrator password
The employee approved push prompts on her phone that she had not started
The firm had switched MFA off for all mailboxes
The attacker stole the employee's phone from her desk
quiz.explanation: The employee entered her password on a phishing page and then approved MFA push prompts four times one evening although she was not logging in. MFA was in place, but the human step defeated it.

quiz.question: What did NYDFS find was the main technique in the July 2020 Twitter hack?
options: Malware hidden in a software update from a vendor
A brute-force attack on Twitter's password database
Phone calls posing as the IT help desk, leading staff to a fake VPN login page
An insider who sold administrator access for bitcoin
quiz.explanation: DFS reported that attackers called employees claiming to be from the IT help desk about VPN problems, sent them to a look-alike login page and got some to approve MFA. It found no malware or sophisticated exploits.

quiz.question: An email from a known supplier asks accounts payable to send future payments to a new bank account and says not to phone because its lines are down. What should the clerk do first?
options: Reply to the email asking for a letter on company letterhead
Update the account, since the email came from the supplier's address
Verify the change by calling the supplier on the number already on file
Forward the email to all colleagues so they know about the change
quiz.explanation: Changed bank details plus a block on calling are signs of business email compromise. Verification must use a trusted channel already on record; replies and letters can be faked by the same attacker.

quiz.question: Kestrel Point updated its risk assessment after a rise in text-message scams targeting staff phones. What does Part 500 imply for this year's awareness training?
options: The training can stay the same as long as it is delivered yearly
Only the IT team needs to hear about the new risk
The training should be updated to cover the newly identified risk
No change is needed until the next DFS examination
quiz.explanation: Part 500 requires awareness training that is updated to reflect risks identified in the entity's risk assessment, so new threats found there belong in the training.

quiz.question: A branch employee clicked a link in a suspicious email and entered her password before realising it was fake. What is the best next step?
options: Delete the email so no one else can click it
Report it immediately so security can reset her credentials and check for misuse
Wait to see if anything unusual happens over the next week
Change her password herself and say nothing to avoid a record
quiz.explanation: Fast reporting lets the security team reset access, review activity and block the campaign. Quietly changing the password misses sessions already opened and other victims.

quiz.question: Under Part 500, which group must receive cybersecurity updates and training sufficient to address relevant cybersecurity risks, in addition to the general awareness training?
options: Board members only
External auditors
Cybersecurity personnel
Customers who use online banking
quiz.explanation: Section 500.10 requires covered entities to provide cybersecurity personnel with updates and training sufficient to address relevant risks, and to verify that key personnel keep their knowledge current.

quiz.question: A bank's phishing test shows a falling click rate but also very few reports of the test email. What is the most useful conclusion?
options: Training should also push staff to report, because detection depends on reports
Reporting does not matter as long as nobody clicks
The tests should stop because staff now recognise phishing
The program is fully effective because fewer people clicked
quiz.explanation: Low reporting means real attacks may go unnoticed until someone clicks. Effective awareness programs measure both clicks and reports, and teach the reporting route.

sessions.title: Access Management and Protecting Customer Information
sessions.summary: Least privilege, privileged accounts, yearly access reviews, prompt removal of leavers, multi-factor authentication, encryption and secure disposal under the federal guidelines and Part 500.
objectives: Apply least privilege and explain the Part 500 access duties, including yearly reviews and prompt removal of access
Explain where Part 500 requires multi-factor authentication and how compensating controls are approved
Link federal access controls, encryption, monitoring and disposal measures to everyday tasks
Recognise the access failures behind real enforcement cases

cards.title: The folder called PASSWORDS
cards.setting: IT audit room, Buffalo operations center.

lines.text: Priya, the access review turned up something ugly. Three branch PCs still share one local admin account, and someone kept a spreadsheet of service passwords on the shared drive.
Encrypted, at least?
Password-protected, in a folder literally named PASSWORDS. Anyone with access to that drive could copy it, including the call center.
That's not my team's spreadsheet, I hope. We just use the logins we were given.
It is nobody's spreadsheet from today. NYDFS fined a consumer lender for exactly this pattern in 2023. Access is where policy meets real life.
Welcome to the Keyholder's Hall. Who gets which keys, for how long, and how we prove it.

scenes.heading: Need to have, not nice to have
scenes.narration: Give each person only the access their job needs. Part 500 says access to systems holding nonpublic information must be limited to what is necessary for the user's job.

scenes.heading: Guard the master keys
scenes.narration: Privileged accounts can change settings and create other accounts. Keep as few as possible, limit what they can do and use them only for tasks that need them.

scenes.heading: Review every year at least
scenes.narration: Covered entities must review all user access at least once a year and remove access that is no longer needed. Many banks review sensitive systems more often.

scenes.heading: Close the door when people leave
scenes.narration: Access must be terminated promptly after someone leaves. Movers matter too: a transfer should remove old access, not just add new access.

scenes.heading: Prove it is really you
scenes.narration: Multi-factor authentication combines at least two of: something you know, something you have, something you are. Part 500 requires it for anyone accessing a covered entity's information systems.

cards.title: Layers of access protection
cards.caption: The top of the pyramid holds the most power, so it gets the most control.

items.label: Privileged accounts
items.detail: Fewest people, tightest limits, monitored activity

items.label: Access to nonpublic information
items.detail: Only what the role needs; reviewed at least yearly

items.label: Multi-factor authentication
items.detail: Required for anyone accessing the entity's systems under Part 500

items.label: Password policy
items.detail: Written policy meeting industry standards where passwords are used

items.label: Joiner, mover, leaver process
items.detail: Grant, change and promptly remove access as people move

cards.question: A loan officer moves from the mortgage team to commercial lending. Which access action best fits Part 500's access duties?
options: Grant the commercial lending access and remove the mortgage access she no longer needs
Add commercial lending access and keep the mortgage access in case she helps out later
Keep all access as is until the yearly access review
Give her a privileged account so she can manage her own permissions
cards.explanation: Part 500 limits access to what the job requires and requires removal of access no longer necessary. Movers who keep old rights build up excess access over time, a common audit finding.

cards.title: The Part 500 access and authentication rules
cards.body:
Section **500.7** requires every covered entity, based on its risk assessment, to:

- limit user access to systems with nonpublic information to what each **job requires**
- limit the **number and functions of privileged accounts**, and use them only when needed
- **review all user access at least once a year** and remove what is no longer necessary
- disable or securely configure protocols that allow **remote control of devices**
- **promptly terminate access** after departures
- keep a **written password policy** that meets industry standards

Class A companies must also use a privileged access management solution and block commonly used passwords.

Section **500.12** requires **multi-factor authentication for any individual accessing any information system** of the covered entity. The CISO may approve equivalent or more secure compensating controls in writing, reviewed at least yearly.

cards.title: Federal guideline or Part 500 detail?
cards.prompt: Both rulebooks expect access controls. Sort each item by where the specific wording comes from.

items.text: Consider access controls that stop employees giving customer data to people seeking it by fraud
Consider dual control, segregation of duties and background checks for staff with access to customer data
Consider encryption of customer information in transit or in storage where unauthorized people may have access
Review all user access privileges at least once a year
Use multi-factor authentication for any individual accessing any information system
Have a written policy requiring encryption of nonpublic information in transit over external networks and at rest
Monitor the activity of authorized users to detect unauthorized access or tampering
Develop measures to dispose of customer and consumer information properly

cards.title: Real case: OneMain Financial and NYDFS (2023)
cards.body:
In May 2023 **NYDFS** settled with OneMain Financial Group, a DFS-licensed consumer lender, for **USD 4.25 million** under Part 500.

DFS described findings from the company's own internal audit:

- access reviews for a network of more than **11,000 users** were done **manually**, with a high risk of error
- local administrator accounts were **shared**, so actions could not be traced to a person
- some accounts still used the **default password** given at onboarding
- passwords were kept in a file in a folder named **'PASSWORDS'** on a shared drive that call center staff could reach

DFS also found gaps in application security, cybersecurity training for personnel and third-party oversight.

**Lesson:** access failures are usually ordinary habits. Shared accounts, default passwords and convenient files are what examiners look for.

cards.title: Real case: optional MFA at PayPal (NYDFS, 2025)
cards.body:
In the **2025 PayPal** settlement, DFS found that the company's own policy required risk-based authentication for activity that gave access to account information, but **multi-factor authentication was optional** for the customer accounts that criminals reached by credential stuffing.

The attackers used passwords stolen elsewhere and tested them automatically. Where customers had reused passwords and had not turned on MFA, the attackers got in and could view tax forms showing **full Social Security numbers**, which an untrained engineering team had left unmasked.

PayPal stopped the automated logins with CAPTCHA and rate limiting, masked the data and forced password resets. DFS still found a violation of the Part 500 duty to use **effective controls against unauthorized access**.

**Lesson:** a control written in a policy only counts when it is switched on.

cards.title: The leaver's account
cards.setting: Grace's office, Brooklyn branch, Monday morning.

lines.text: Quick one. A teller left on Friday after a dispute with her supervisor. HR said they'd tell IT 'this week'. Is that OK?
Her credentials still work on the teller platform and her VPN token is active. 'This week' is too slow.
Part 500 says access must be terminated promptly after departures. A departure after a dispute is exactly when to act fastest.
I didn't know I was part of this. I thought access was IT's problem.
Managers start the process. IT can only remove what it knows about.

cards.title: Closing the leaver's access
cards.situation: You are the security analyst on duty. The teller's access is still live three days after she left, and the core system shows a login from her account at 7:10 am today from an unfamiliar device.

choices.text: Disable all her accounts and tokens now, preserve the logs and escalate the 7:10 am login as a possible incident.
choices.outcome: Right. Prompt termination is a Part 500 duty, and the login after departure may mean misuse. Preserving logs keeps evidence for the incident team, which will judge whether any notice is needed.

choices.text: Disable her accounts now, but treat the login as a glitch since she has left the bank.
choices.outcome: Half right. Removing access is correct, but a login after departure is a warning sign that needs investigation, not an assumption. Customer information may have been viewed.

choices.text: Wait for HR's formal ticket so the change is properly documented.
choices.outcome: Paperwork matters, but it cannot justify leaving active access for a leaver, especially with suspicious activity. Document after you act.

choices.text: Reset her password and send the new one to her personal email so she can return any bank files.
choices.outcome: This keeps the account alive and sends a credential outside the bank. It increases risk instead of removing it.

cards.title: Access risk at a glance
cards.caption: Monitoring, MFA strength and review frequency should rise as you move toward the top right.

items.label: Watch closely
items.detail: Low privilege, highly sensitive data: tellers and call center agents viewing customer records

items.label: Highest risk
items.detail: High privilege, highly sensitive data: database and core system administrators

items.label: Baseline controls
items.detail: Low privilege, low sensitivity: intranet and general office tools

items.label: Guard the keys
items.detail: High privilege, low sensitivity data: network and directory administrators who can grant access

cards.title: A clean joiner-mover-leaver cycle
cards.prompt: Put the steps of access management for one employee in a sensible order.
steps: Manager requests access based on the role's documented needs
Access owner approves and IT grants only the listed rights, with MFA enrolled
Activity on sensitive systems is monitored as the risk assessment requires
On a transfer, old access is removed and new role access is granted
Yearly (or more frequent) review confirms each right is still needed
On departure, all accounts, tokens and remote access are disabled promptly

cards.title: Protecting customer information day to day

cards.back: Lock away printed customer records and lock your screen whenever you step away.
Send customer information only through approved, encrypted channels, never personal email or messaging apps.
Shred paper and use approved wiping for media. Both rulebooks expect secure disposal of customer information.
Never share logins. Shared accounts hide who did what and break audit trails.
If someone asks for access 'just in case', ask what task it supports. Least privilege protects them too.

cards.question: Under Part 500, who may approve a compensating control in place of multi-factor authentication?
options: Any system owner, verbally, if the system is old
The help desk manager, for up to three months
The CISO, in writing, with the control reviewed at least once a year
No one; Part 500 allows no alternatives to MFA in any case
cards.explanation: Section 500.12(b) lets a covered entity's CISO approve reasonably equivalent or more secure compensating controls in writing, and requires them to be reviewed periodically and at least yearly.

cards.title: Stage three takeaways
items: Give each person only the access the job needs, and keep privileged accounts few, limited and used only when needed
Part 500 requires a review of all user access at least yearly and prompt termination of access after departures
Part 500 requires MFA for anyone accessing a covered entity's systems; only the CISO can approve written alternatives
Federal guidelines expect access controls, encryption, dual control, monitoring and secure disposal where the risk assessment calls for them
Shared accounts, default passwords and convenient password files are recurring enforcement findings

cards.prompt: List the systems you can access today. Is there any access you no longer use? Who would you ask to remove it, and how quickly would your access end if you left tomorrow?

quiz.question: Under Part 500, how often at minimum must a covered entity review all user access privileges?
options: Only when an employee leaves
Only after a cybersecurity incident
At least once a year
Every three years
quiz.explanation: Section 500.7(a)(4) requires a periodic review, at minimum annual, of all user access privileges and removal of access that is no longer necessary.

quiz.question: A database administrator uses her privileged account to read email and browse the web all day. Which Part 500 principle does this break?
options: Privileged accounts must be shared within the team
Privileged accounts must be reviewed every month
Privileged accounts should be used only for functions that need that access
Privileged users are exempt from MFA
quiz.explanation: Part 500 requires covered entities to limit the use of privileged accounts to when performing functions that need such access. Everyday use widens the damage if the account is compromised by phishing.

quiz.question: Which control does the federal Interagency Guidelines list among measures a bank must consider for employees with access to customer information?
options: Dual control, segregation of duties and background checks
Rotating all staff between branches monthly
Banning remote work for all employees
Mandatory polygraph tests every year
quiz.explanation: Paragraph III.C.1 lists dual control procedures, segregation of duties and employee background checks for staff with responsibilities for or access to customer information.

quiz.question: What did NYDFS find about passwords at OneMain Financial in its 2023 consent order?
options: Customers' passwords were sold to a vendor
Passwords were kept in a file in a folder named 'PASSWORDS' on a widely accessible shared drive
Passwords were changed every day, which overloaded the help desk
The company used biometrics instead of passwords for all staff
quiz.explanation: DFS cited internal audit findings that passwords were stored on a shared drive in a folder named 'PASSWORDS', reachable by staff including the call center, along with shared admin accounts and default passwords.

quiz.question: A covered entity's legacy teller system cannot support multi-factor authentication. What does Part 500 allow?
options: DFS must approve the system before it is used again
The business line head may sign a permanent waiver
The CISO may approve equivalent or more secure compensating controls in writing, reviewed at least yearly
The system can run without extra controls because it is legacy
quiz.explanation: Section 500.12(b) allows the CISO to approve reasonably equivalent or more secure compensating controls in writing, reviewed periodically and at least annually.

quiz.question: An employee resigns and leaves on Friday. Under Part 500, when should her access be removed?
options: At the next yearly access review
Only if she is believed to be a security risk
Within 90 days, when HR closes the file
Promptly after her departure
quiz.explanation: Part 500 requires covered entities to promptly terminate access following departures. Waiting for a review cycle or a risk judgement leaves an open door.

quiz.question: Why do shared administrator accounts worry examiners, as in the OneMain case?
options: They cost more in software licences
They prevent the use of encryption
They make it impossible to tell which person carried out an action
They are slower than individual accounts
quiz.explanation: Shared accounts break accountability: logs show the account, not the person. DFS noted that shared local admin accounts compromised the ability to identify malicious actors.

quiz.question: Kestrel Point wants to stop customer records leaving by personal email. Which Part 500 duty most directly supports monitoring for this?
options: The April 15 yearly compliance filing
The definition of a Class A company
The 72-hour incident notice to DFS
Risk-based controls to monitor authorized users' activity and detect unauthorized access or use of nonpublic information
quiz.explanation: Section 500.14(a)(1) requires risk-based policies, procedures and controls to monitor authorized users and detect unauthorized access, use or tampering with nonpublic information.

quiz.question: Under Part 500, which statement about encryption of nonpublic information is accurate?
options: Encryption is optional and left to each business line
A written policy must require encryption in transit over external networks and at rest, with CISO-approved alternatives if at-rest encryption is infeasible
Only data sent to regulators must be encrypted
Encryption is required at rest but never in transit
quiz.explanation: Section 500.15 requires a written encryption policy meeting industry standards for nonpublic information in transit over external networks and at rest, with written CISO approval of compensating controls where encryption at rest is infeasible.

quiz.question: What was the main access control failure DFS cited in the 2025 PayPal settlement?
options: Staff badges did not open the data center doors
Multi-factor authentication was optional for affected customer accounts
Administrators were locked out of their own accounts
The company used too many security tools
quiz.explanation: DFS found that MFA was optional for the customer accounts reached through credential stuffing, despite PayPal's policy calling for risk-based authentication, and cited the duty to use effective controls against unauthorized access.

sessions.title: Incidents: Response Programs, the 36-Hour Rule and the 72-Hour Notice
sessions.summary: How a bank responds to unauthorized access to customer information, when the federal 36-hour notice and the NYDFS 72-hour notice apply, what service providers must tell banks, and when customers are notified.
objectives: Describe the elements of a federal response program for unauthorized access to customer information, including customer notice
Decide whether an event is a computer-security incident and a notification incident under the 36-hour rule
Apply the Part 500 definitions of cybersecurity event and incident, the 72-hour notice and the extortion payment notices
Explain the bank service provider's four-hour disruption notice and Part 500's incident plan and testing duties

cards.title: Saturday, 2:14 am
cards.setting: Incident bridge call. Tomas in Buffalo, Priya at home in Queens, Ellen joining later.

lines.text: Our online banking provider just called. Ransomware hit their data center. Customers have been unable to log in for two hours and they don't know when it comes back.
Is our own network affected? And has any customer data left their systems?
No sign it reached us. Data exfiltration unknown. They say a full forensic answer could take days.

Then two clocks may be ticking. The Fed's 36-hour clock starts when we determine it is a notification incident. DFS's 72-hour clock starts when we determine it is a cybersecurity incident, and an incident at a service provider counts.
So who decides, and when?
We decide, using our incident plan, and we write down when and why. Welcome to the Clock Tower.

scenes.heading: Federal: the 36-hour rule
scenes.narration: Since 2022, every banking organization supervised by the OCC, the Fed or the FDIC must notify its primary federal regulator of a notification incident as soon as possible, and no later than 36 hours after determining one has occurred. Email or phone is enough; it is an early warning, not a full report.

scenes.heading: Federal: service providers
scenes.narration: A bank service provider must tell each affected bank as soon as possible when an incident has disrupted, or is likely to disrupt, covered services for four or more hours. Scheduled maintenance the bank was told about does not count.

scenes.heading: New York: the 72-hour notice
scenes.narration: A NYDFS covered entity must notify DFS electronically as promptly as possible, and no later than 72 hours after determining a cybersecurity incident has occurred at the entity, its affiliates or a third-party service provider.

scenes.heading: Customers
scenes.narration: Under the federal response program guidance, when sensitive customer information is accessed without authority, the bank investigates promptly and notifies affected customers as soon as possible if misuse has occurred or is reasonably possible.

scenes.heading: And more
scenes.narration: State breach notice laws, suspicious activity reports and law enforcement contacts may also apply. Your incident plan pulls these together so nothing is missed.

cards.title: Federal 36-hour notice and NYDFS 72-hour notice
cards.caption: A New York-chartered bank may owe both notices for the same event, each on its own clock.

items.label: Who
items.left: Banks and holding companies supervised by the OCC, the Fed or the FDIC

items.label: Trigger
items.left: A notification incident: actual harm that materially disrupts or is likely to disrupt key operations
items.right: A cybersecurity incident: an event that requires notice to a government body, is likely to cause material harm, or deploys ransomware

items.label: Deadline
items.left: As soon as possible, no later than 36 hours after determining
items.right: As promptly as possible, no later than 72 hours after determining

items.label: To whom
items.left: Primary federal regulator's supervisory office or designated contact
items.right: The Superintendent, electronically, using the DFS form

items.label: Third parties
items.left: Service providers must alert bank customers of 4+ hour disruptions
items.right: Incidents at a third-party service provider count for the covered entity

cards.question: When does the federal 36-hour clock start?
options: When the bank determines that a notification incident has occurred
When the attacker first enters the network
When the bank's board is informed
When the forensic investigation is complete
cards.explanation: The rule requires notice as soon as possible and no later than 36 hours after the banking organization determines a notification incident has occurred. Waiting for full forensics would defeat its early-warning purpose.

cards.title: Federal definitions that decide the 36-hour notice
cards.body:
The 2021 rule (OCC, Fed and FDIC, 86 FR 66424) uses two steps.

A **computer-security incident** is an occurrence that causes **actual harm** to the confidentiality, integrity or availability of an information system or the information it holds. A failed attempt is not one.

A **notification incident** is a computer-security incident that has **materially disrupted or degraded**, or is **reasonably likely** to, the bank's:

- ability to carry out banking operations or deliver products and services to a **material portion of its customers**
- **business lines** whose failure would cause a material loss of revenue, profit or franchise value
- operations whose failure would **threaten US financial stability**

Only notification incidents trigger the 36-hour notice. The rule's examples include a large denial-of-service attack that blocks customer access for an extended period, and hacking that disables operations for an extended period.

cards.title: Which notice could it trigger?
cards.prompt: Kestrel Point (a New York-chartered Fed member bank) faces these events. Sort each by the most likely outcome.

items.text: Ransomware locks the core banking system and branches cannot serve customers for a day
A denial-of-service attack takes online banking down for most customers for many hours
Ransomware hits a material part of the HR systems; banking services are not disrupted or likely to be
An event that requires the bank to notify a state attorney general under a breach law, with no disruption
A phishing email is blocked by the filter and nobody clicks
A failed login attempt from abroad is stopped by MFA

cards.title: The federal response program for customer information
cards.body:
The interagency guidance on **response programs** (Supplement A to the guidelines) expects every bank's program to cover unauthorized access to customer information. As the Fed's compliance guide summarises it, the program should include:

- **assessing** the nature and scope of the incident and what customer information was accessed or misused
- **notifying the primary federal regulator** promptly once the bank becomes aware of unauthorized access to **sensitive customer information**
- notifying **law enforcement**, in addition to filing a timely **SAR**, where federal crimes need immediate attention
- **containing** the incident while **preserving records and evidence**
- **notifying customers** when warranted

**Sensitive customer information** means a name, address or phone number together with a Social Security, driver's license, account or card number, or a PIN or password giving account access; or any combination, such as a user name and password, that lets someone into the account.

cards.title: Customer notice under the federal guidance

cards.back: Once it becomes aware of unauthorized access to sensitive customer information, it conducts a reasonable investigation to promptly judge the likelihood of misuse.
If misuse has occurred or is reasonably possible, the bank notifies affected customers as soon as possible.
Yes, if an appropriate law enforcement agency decides notice would hinder a criminal investigation and asks in writing. Notice follows once it no longer interferes.

cards.front: Is a name plus account number sensitive?
cards.back: Yes. A name, address or phone number combined with an account or card number is sensitive customer information.

cards.front: What about a user name and password?
cards.back: Yes. Any combination that would let an unauthorized person access the account electronically counts.

cards.title: Real case: an incident nobody investigated (NYDFS, 2021)
cards.body:
Back to **Residential Mortgage Services** (DFS consent order, March 2021, **USD 1.5 million**). After the 2019 phishing compromise of an employee's mailbox, IT blocked the intruder but **did not investigate** what the mailbox held, although the employee handled Social Security and bank account numbers every day.

Because no one checked, the firm could not tell which consumers were affected and **sent no breach notices** to consumers, state agencies or DFS. Part 500 then required notice to DFS within **72 hours** of determining that a cybersecurity event needing notice to another government body had occurred.

Only after DFS examiners asked did the firm hire outside experts, review every email in the account and notify affected consumers, offering credit monitoring, by late 2020.

**Lesson:** blocking the attacker is the start of incident response, not the end. You cannot meet a notice deadline for an impact you never assessed.

cards.title: Two hours later on the bridge

lines.text: Update: the provider now says online banking will be down at least 24 hours. That's most of our retail customers locked out.
Then I am determining that this is a notification incident under the federal rule and a cybersecurity incident under Part 500. Log the time: 4:21 am.
Ellen here. Do we notify now, or wait until we know whether data was stolen?
Now. The Fed notice can be a call or email to our supervisory contact. DFS gets its electronic notice too. We keep both updated as facts change.
And customers?
If we find sensitive customer information was accessed and misuse is reasonably possible, they get notice as soon as possible. That decision comes from the investigation.

cards.title: The ransom note
cards.situation: A day later the attackers email Kestrel Point directly, threatening to publish customer files unless the bank pays. A senior executive suggests quietly paying through a crypto broker 'so the regulators never need to know'.

choices.text: Pay quietly; if the data never appears, no further notices are needed.
choices.outcome: This breaks Part 500. A covered entity that makes an extortion payment must notify DFS within 24 hours of payment and explain within 30 days why it paid, the alternatives considered and its sanctions diligence, including OFAC. Secrecy is not an option.

choices.text: Refuse to discuss payment at all and stop updating regulators until the threat passes.
choices.outcome: Declining to pay can be a sound decision, but going quiet is not. Part 500 imposes a continuing duty to update DFS with material changes, and the federal supervisor should be kept informed.

choices.text: Escalate under the incident plan to legal, the board and law enforcement, keep DFS and the Fed updated, and follow the Part 500 extortion payment notices if any payment is ever made.
choices.outcome: Right. The plan sets who decides. If a payment is made, DFS must be told within 24 hours and given a written explanation within 30 days, including diligence on sanctions rules.

cards.title: Kestrel Point's incident clocks
cards.caption: Clocks run from determination, so the incident plan must say who determines and how it is recorded.

items.label: Provider calls
items.detail: Service provider reports a ransomware disruption; triage starts

items.label: Determination
items.detail: CISO determines a notification incident and a cybersecurity incident; time logged

items.label: Federal notice
items.detail: Fed supervisory contact told by email or phone, as soon as possible

items.label: DFS notice
items.detail: Electronic notice to DFS, then continuing updates

items.label: Customer notice
items.detail: If sensitive data was accessed and misuse is reasonably possible

items.label: If a ransom is paid
items.detail: DFS notice of payment, then written reasons and diligence

cards.title: A Part 500 incident response plan in action
cards.prompt: Put these response steps in a sensible order.
steps: Detect and triage the event using the roles and decision rights set in the plan
Contain the threat while preserving logs and evidence
Determine whether a reportable incident has occurred and record the time
Send the required regulator notices and keep them updated
Recover systems, including restoring from backups
Prepare a root cause analysis and update the plan and training

cards.question: Under Part 500, which event is a 'cybersecurity incident' even if no customer data was taken?
options: A phishing email that the filter blocked
Ransomware deployed within a material part of the covered entity's information systems
An unsuccessful attempt to guess an administrator's password
A scheduled software update that was announced in advance
cards.explanation: Part 500 defines a cybersecurity incident to include an event that results in ransomware being deployed within a material part of the entity's systems, as well as events requiring notice to a government body or likely to cause material harm.

cards.title: Make the clocks workable before you need them
cards.body:
- **Name the decision-maker** who determines an incident, and a backup, in the incident plan.
- **Keep regulator contacts current**: the Fed, OCC or FDIC supervisory contact and the DFS portal access.
- **Give service providers a bank point of contact** so their four-hour disruption notices reach someone at 2 am.
- **Test yearly**: Part 500 requires covered entities to test incident response and continuity plans, and backup restoration, at least once a year.
- **Train the responders**: Part 500 requires training for employees responsible for carrying out the plans.

cards.title: Stage four takeaways
items: Federally supervised banks notify their primary federal regulator no later than 36 hours after determining a notification incident
Bank service providers must alert affected banks as soon as possible of incidents disrupting covered services for four or more hours
NYDFS covered entities notify DFS no later than 72 hours after determining a cybersecurity incident, including one at a third-party service provider
Under the federal response program guidance, customers are notified as soon as possible when misuse of sensitive information has occurred or is reasonably possible
Part 500 requires DFS notice within 24 hours of any extortion payment and a written explanation within 30 days

cards.prompt: If your bank's main system went down tonight, who would determine whether it is a reportable incident, and how would you reach them? Find the answer in your incident plan.

quiz.question: Under the federal rule, what must a bank do after determining a notification incident has occurred?
options: File a full forensic report with FinCEN within 30 days
Notify every customer by mail within 36 hours
Inform the FFIEC within 72 hours
Notify its primary federal regulator as soon as possible and no later than 36 hours later
quiz.explanation: The rule requires notice to the primary federal regulator's supervisory office or designated contact as soon as possible and no later than 36 hours after determination. It is an early alert, not a full report.

quiz.question: Which event is NOT a computer-security incident under the federal rule?
options: A blocked attempt that caused no actual harm to any system or data
A denial-of-service attack that takes online banking offline
A hack that alters customer account balances
Ransomware that encrypts a branch file server
quiz.explanation: A computer-security incident requires actual harm to the confidentiality, integrity or availability of a system or its information. An unsuccessful attempt causing no harm does not qualify.

quiz.question: A bank's card processor suffers an attack and expects card services to be degraded for six hours. What must the processor do under the federal rule?
options: Do nothing, because only banks have notice duties
Notify a bank-designated point of contact at each affected bank as soon as possible
Wait until the disruption ends and then send a summary
Notify the bank's primary federal regulator directly within 36 hours
quiz.explanation: Bank service providers must notify at least one bank-designated contact at each affected banking organization as soon as possible when an incident has disrupted or is likely to disrupt covered services for four or more hours.

quiz.question: A NYDFS covered entity learns its outsourced payroll provider suffered a cybersecurity incident that affects the entity. The provider says it has already told DFS. What must the covered entity do?
options: Nothing, because the provider's notice covers it
Wait for DFS to contact it
Notify only the Federal Reserve
Notify DFS itself within 72 hours of determining the incident occurred
quiz.explanation: Part 500.17(a) covers incidents at the entity, its affiliates or a third-party service provider, and DFS's FAQ confirms the covered entity must notify even if the provider also does.

quiz.question: Under the federal response program guidance, when should a bank notify affected customers after unauthorized access to sensitive customer information?
options: Within 36 hours, in every case
As soon as possible once it determines misuse has occurred or is reasonably possible
Only if a court orders it
Only after the attacker has been arrested
quiz.explanation: After a reasonable investigation to promptly assess the likelihood of misuse, the bank should notify affected customers as soon as possible if misuse has occurred or is reasonably possible.

quiz.question: Which data set is 'sensitive customer information' under the federal response program guidance?
options: A customer's name and the city where she lives
A customer's name together with her debit card number
The average credit score of all customers in a region
A list of the bank's branch addresses
quiz.explanation: Sensitive customer information is a name, address or phone number combined with items such as a Social Security, driver's license, account or card number, or a PIN or password; or any combination allowing account access.

quiz.question: A covered entity pays a ransom to regain access to its systems. What does Part 500 require?
options: Approval from DFS before any payment is made
Notice to DFS only if the payment exceeds a set threshold
No notice, since the incident itself was already reported
Notice to DFS within 24 hours of payment and a written explanation within 30 days
quiz.explanation: Section 500.17(c) requires notice of an extortion payment within 24 hours and, within 30 days, a written description of why it was necessary, alternatives considered and diligence, including on OFAC rules.

quiz.question: What was the central failure in the Residential Mortgage Services case regarding incident response?
options: IT blocked the intruder but never checked what customer data the mailbox held, so no notices were sent
The firm reported the event to the wrong federal agency
The firm notified customers too early, before DFS approved
The firm paid a ransom without telling DFS
quiz.explanation: DFS found the firm failed to investigate which consumer data was exposed, so it could not send required breach notices to consumers, state agencies or DFS within 72 hours. The event surfaced during an exam about 18 months later.

quiz.question: Under Part 500, how often must a covered entity test its incident response and business continuity plans?
options: Whenever DFS requests a test
Every three years
Only after a real incident
At least once a year, including its ability to restore from backups
quiz.explanation: Section 500.16(d) requires periodic, at minimum annual, testing of incident response and BCDR plans with critical staff and management, and of the ability to restore critical data and systems from backups.

quiz.question: A law enforcement agency asks a bank in writing to delay customer notice because it would hinder a criminal investigation. What does the federal guidance allow?
options: Delay the notice, then notify customers once it will no longer interfere
Cancel customer notice permanently
Delay only if the bank's board votes to do so
Notify customers anyway, since the bank's duty overrides the request
quiz.explanation: The response program guidance recognises a delay when an appropriate law enforcement agency determines notice would interfere with a criminal investigation and asks in writing; notice follows as soon as it will no longer interfere.

sessions.title: Third Parties, Board Oversight and Exam Readiness
sessions.summary: Overseeing service providers under the federal guidelines and Part 500, how the board and the CISO govern the program, the April 15 DFS filing, testing and records, and how examiners judge the whole program.
objectives: Explain the federal service provider duties and the Part 500 third-party service provider policy in general terms
Describe the board's role under the federal guidelines and Part 500, including yearly reports and sufficient understanding
Explain the NYDFS April 15 certification or acknowledgment, who signs it and how long records are kept
Prepare evidence of training, testing and oversight for a federal or DFS examination

cards.title: The vendor that started early
cards.setting: Third-party risk office, Manhattan. Two weeks before the exams.
