lines.text: Bad news. Marketing signed a new analytics vendor last month. They already have a feed of customer data, and our security questionnaire is still 'pending'.
So customer information is flowing to a provider we haven't assessed. That's the OneMain pattern DFS cited in 2023.
The contract also has no clause on telling us about security incidents.
Ellen Whitaker. I chair the board risk committee. I'll be asking about this at our meeting, and so will the examiners.
Then let's fix it properly. Final stage: the Boardroom Summit. Third parties, the board, and proving it all to the examiners.

scenes.heading: You can outsource work, not responsibility
scenes.narration: Banks rely on providers for core systems, cloud, cards and more. Under both rulebooks, the bank stays responsible for protecting its customer information wherever it sits.

scenes.heading: Federal: select, contract, monitor
scenes.narration: The federal guidelines require due diligence when selecting service providers, contracts that require them to protect customer information, and monitoring where the risk assessment calls for it, for example by reviewing their audits and test results.

scenes.heading: New York: a written policy
scenes.narration: Part 500 requires written third-party policies based on risk: identify and assess providers, set minimum security practices, do due diligence and reassess them periodically.

scenes.heading: What contracts should cover
scenes.narration: Part 500's guidelines point to access controls and multi-factor authentication, encryption, prompt notice of cybersecurity events affecting the entity, and representations about the provider's security.

scenes.heading: The wider guidance
scenes.narration: The 2023 interagency guidance on third-party relationships describes the full life cycle, from planning and due diligence to contracts, ongoing monitoring and exit.

cards.title: Third-party life cycle in brief
cards.caption: Based in general terms on the 2023 interagency third-party guidance and Part 500.11.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Decide if outsourcing fits; identify data and systems the provider will touch

items.label: Due diligence
items.detail: Assess security practices before any data flows, scaled to risk

items.label: Contract
items.detail: Security duties, MFA and encryption, incident notice, audit rights

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: Review audits, test results and incidents; reassess risk ratings

items.label: Exit
items.detail: Retrieve or destroy data and remove access when the relationship ends

cards.question: Under the federal guidelines, which duty does a bank have toward a service provider that handles customer information?
options: Approve the provider's own board members
Run the provider's security operations itself
Report the provider's annual revenue to its regulator
Require it by contract to implement appropriate measures to protect customer information
cards.explanation: Paragraph III.D requires due diligence in selecting providers, contracts requiring appropriate safeguards, and monitoring where the risk assessment indicates, including reviewing audits or test summaries.

cards.title: The board and the CISO
cards.body:
**Federal guidelines (all banks).** The board or a board committee must **approve** the written program and **oversee** it, assigning responsibility and reviewing management reports. Management must report to the board **at least once a year** on the program's status and compliance, covering items such as the risk assessment, risk decisions, service provider arrangements, **test results**, **security breaches and responses** and recommended changes.

**Part 500 (covered entities).** The **CISO** reports **in writing at least once a year** to the senior governing body on the program, material risks, its effectiveness, material events and plans to fix material gaps, and reports **significant events promptly**. The senior governing body must:

- have **sufficient understanding** of cybersecurity to oversee it, using advisors if needed
- require management to develop and maintain the program
- **regularly receive and review** management reports
- confirm management has given the program **sufficient resources**

cards.title: Who does what in governance?
cards.prompt: Match each role to its duty.

pairs.right: Approves the written information security program and oversees its implementation
Reports at least yearly to the board on program status and compliance with the guidelines
Reports in writing at least yearly to the senior governing body and promptly on significant events
Sign the yearly DFS certification or acknowledgment
Conduct or review tests of key controls, separate from those who build or run the program

cards.title: Real case: the board's role at Capital One (OCC, 2020)
cards.body:
The **OCC's 2020** action against Capital One is a governance case as much as a technology case. Besides the **USD 80 million** penalty, a separate cease-and-desist order required the board to appoint a **compliance committee** with a majority of directors who were not employees or officers, to meet at least quarterly and to report progress to the board.

The OCC's findings explain why: internal audit had not reported weaknesses clearly to the audit committee, and when concerns were raised, the **board did not hold management accountable**.

**Lesson:** under the federal guidelines the board does more than approve a document. Examiners look at what reports it received, what questions it asked and whether problems were followed through.

cards.title: Real case: vendors and NYDFS at OneMain (2023)
cards.body:
In the **2023 OneMain** settlement (**USD 4.25 million**), DFS found that the company had a vendor management policy that assigned risk ratings, but did not complete due diligence on time for some **high- and medium-risk vendors**. Some vendors **started work before** the security questionnaire and risk acceptance were finished.

After several cybersecurity events caused by vendors' poor handling of nonpublic information, OneMain ended those relationships but **did not adjust their risk scores** or improve its own third-party procedures.

**Lesson:** a vendor policy only works if the steps happen before data flows, and if lessons from vendor incidents feed back into the process.

cards.title: The board risk committee
cards.setting: Board risk committee meeting, 30th floor, Manhattan.

lines.text: Priya, your written report says awareness training completion is 97%. Who are the other 3%, and what access do they have?
Mostly new joiners in their first month and two contractors. The contractors' access is suspended until they finish.
Good. And the analytics vendor Kenji mentioned?
Data feed paused, assessment done this week, contract amended to add incident notice and encryption terms.
That's the kind of answer I can defend to examiners. I want it in the minutes.

cards.title: The April 15 filing
cards.situation: It is early April. The CISO's draft DFS filing certifies material compliance with Part 500 for last year. But the yearly access review for two legacy systems was never finished, and the incident response plan was not tested last year.

choices.text: Sign the certification anyway; the gaps are small and will be fixed this year.
choices.outcome: Risky and wrong. A certification must rest on data and documentation showing material compliance. Certifying over known gaps can itself be a violation and damages the entity's credibility with DFS.

choices.text: File an acknowledgment of noncompliance naming the sections not met, describing the gaps and giving a remediation timeline, signed by the highest-ranking executive and the CISO.
choices.outcome: Right. Part 500 gives two options: certify material compliance, or acknowledge noncompliance, identify the sections and give a remediation plan. Supporting records are kept for five years.

choices.text: Skip this year's filing until the gaps are closed.
choices.outcome: Not allowed. Every covered entity must submit either a certification or an acknowledgment by April 15 each year.

choices.text: Ask the business lines to sign instead, since the gaps are theirs.
choices.outcome: Wrong signers. Part 500 requires the highest-ranking executive and the CISO (or the senior officer responsible for the program if there is no CISO) to sign.

cards.title: The governance calendar
cards.caption: Part 500 figures from 23 NYCRR 500.4 and 500.17; federal figure from the Interagency Guidelines.

items.label: Board report (federal)
items.detail: Management reports program status and compliance to the board or committee

items.label: CISO written report
items.detail: To the senior governing body under Part 500

items.label: DFS filing
items.detail: Certification or acknowledgment for the prior calendar year

items.label: Supporting records
items.detail: Kept for DFS to examine after each filing

cards.title: Evidence an examiner would ask for
cards.prompt: Which evidence best supports each area?

items.text: Completion records for yearly awareness training, by person
Course content updated after the latest risk assessment
Records of role training for incident responders and security staff
Penetration test and vulnerability scan reports with remediation tracking
Reviews of service providers' audit reports and test results
Results of the yearly incident response and backup restoration test
Board minutes approving the program and discussing the yearly report
Signed DFS certification or acknowledgment with supporting documents

cards.back: Independent third parties or staff independent of those who develop or maintain the program, at a frequency set by the risk assessment (federal guidelines).

cards.front: How is a Part 500 violation counted?
cards.back: A single prohibited act or failure is a violation, including a material failure to comply with any section for any 24-hour period.

cards.front: Does DFS consider frameworks like NIST?
cards.back: Yes. Alignment with nationally recognised frameworks such as NIST is one of the factors DFS weighs when setting a penalty.

cards.front: Can the CISO work for an affiliate or vendor?
cards.back: Yes under Part 500, but the covered entity keeps responsibility and names a senior person to oversee the provider.

cards.front: Does the program ever stay fixed?
cards.back: No. The federal guidelines require adjusting it for changes in technology, threats, outsourcing and business arrangements.

cards.question: Which statement about the Part 500 yearly filing is correct?
options: It is optional for banks that the Federal Reserve also supervises
It is either a certification of material compliance or an acknowledgment of noncompliance with a remediation plan
It must be signed by the external auditor and the board chair
It is filed every three years with the 72-hour notice log
cards.explanation: Section 500.17(b) requires a yearly submission by April 15: a certification or an acknowledgment identifying the sections not complied with and a remediation timeline, signed by the highest-ranking executive and the CISO.

cards.title: Stage five takeaways
items: Banks stay responsible for customer information held by providers: due diligence, protective contract terms and risk-based monitoring
Part 500 requires written third-party policies, including terms on MFA, encryption and incident notice
The federal board approves and oversees the program and receives a report at least yearly
Part 500 adds a written yearly CISO report and a board with sufficient understanding that confirms resources
By April 15 each covered entity certifies compliance or acknowledges gaps, signed by its top executive and CISO, keeping records five years

cards.prompt: If an examiner asked you tomorrow to prove you completed this year's security training and know how to report an incident, what evidence would you show?

quiz.question: Under the federal guidelines, how often must management report to the board on the information security program?
options: Every quarter, by regulation
Only when a breach occurs
Every three years, before the exam
At least once a year
quiz.explanation: Paragraph III.F requires a report to the board or an appropriate committee at least annually on the program's overall status and compliance with the guidelines.

quiz.question: Who must sign the yearly Part 500 certification or acknowledgment?
options: Any two directors of the board
The highest-ranking executive and the CISO
The head of compliance alone
The board chair and the external auditor
quiz.explanation: Section 500.17(b)(2) requires the filing to be signed by the covered entity's highest-ranking executive and its CISO, or the senior officer responsible for the program if there is no CISO.

quiz.question: A covered entity knows it did not complete its yearly access reviews last year. What should its April 15 submission be?
options: A letter asking DFS to waive the requirement for that year
An acknowledgment identifying the sections not met and a remediation timeline
A certification of compliance, with the gap fixed quietly afterwards
No submission until the reviews are complete
quiz.explanation: Part 500 offers an acknowledgment for entities that did not materially comply, identifying the sections, describing the gaps and giving a remediation timeline. Certifying over known gaps is not supported by the evidence.

quiz.question: Which of these is a duty of the senior governing body under Part 500?
options: Confirming that management has allocated sufficient resources to the cybersecurity program
Writing the technical firewall rules
Personally approving every user access request
Submitting the 72-hour notice to DFS
quiz.explanation: Section 500.4(d) requires the senior governing body to have sufficient understanding, require management to maintain the program, regularly review reports and confirm sufficient resources.

quiz.question: A business unit wants a new vendor to start receiving customer data before the security assessment is complete. Based on the OneMain case and Part 500, what is the best response?
options: Allow it, because the contract can be fixed later
Hold the data until due diligence is done, scaled to the vendor's risk
Allow it for low-risk data, and for any other data too if the deadline is close
Allow it if the vendor promises in an email to be secure
quiz.explanation: Part 500 requires due diligence on third-party providers' cybersecurity practices, and DFS cited OneMain for letting vendors start before security reviews were complete. Assessment should precede data flows.

quiz.question: Under Part 500, which contract topic should third-party policies address?
options: Notice to the covered entity of cybersecurity events affecting its systems or nonpublic information
The provider's staff dress code
The provider's marketing budget
The provider's share price targets
quiz.explanation: Section 500.11(b) lists guidelines for due diligence and contract terms, including access controls and MFA, encryption, notice of cybersecurity events affecting the entity, and representations and warranties about security.

quiz.question: How long must a covered entity keep the records supporting its yearly certification or acknowledgment?
options: Five years
One year
Ten years
Until the next DFS examination only
quiz.explanation: Section 500.17(b)(3) requires covered entities to keep all supporting records, schedules and documentation for five years for DFS examination.

quiz.question: In the OCC's 2020 Capital One cease-and-desist order, what did the board have to set up?
options: A new subsidiary to run its cloud operations
A dedicated hotline to the OCC staffed by directors
A crypto reserve to cover future penalties
A compliance committee with a majority of directors who were not bank employees or officers
quiz.explanation: The order required a compliance committee of at least three members, a majority of them directors who were not employees or officers, meeting at least quarterly to oversee compliance with the order.

quiz.question: Under the federal guidelines, who should conduct or review tests of the key controls of the information security program?
options: Independent third parties or staff independent of those who develop or maintain the program
The same engineers who built the controls, for efficiency
The bank's marketing team, as an outside view
The primary federal regulator, every year
quiz.explanation: Paragraph III.C.3 says tests should be conducted or reviewed by independent third parties or staff independent of those who develop or maintain the security program, at a frequency set by the risk assessment.

quiz.question: Under Part 500, what counts as a violation?
options: A single prohibited act or failure, including a material failure to comply with a section for any 24-hour period
Only violations that DFS finds during an on-site exam
Only a breach that leads to customer losses
Only failures that continue for more than a year
quiz.explanation: Section 500.20(b) states that one prohibited act or failure is a violation, including failure to secure nonpublic information due to noncompliance and material failure to comply for any 24-hour period.

regulators: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS)

references.title: Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards (12 CFR 208, Appendix D-2; Federal Reserve Regulatory Service)
references.provision: Sections II and III (III.C.2 staff training, III.D service providers, III.F annual board report)
references.note: Written information security program approved and overseen by the board, risk assessment, controls, staff training, testing, service provider oversight and an at least annual report to the board; the text is common to all three banking agencies.

references.title: Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards: Small-Entity Compliance Guide
references.note: Explains the guidelines, including training staff to resist pretext calling and other fraud, and the response program guidance: notice to the primary federal regulator, SAR and law enforcement, containment and customer notice when misuse is likely.

references.title: Appendix B to Part 364: Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards
references.note: FDIC version of the same guidelines for state non-member banks (host blocks automated access; text confirmed through the Federal Reserve copy).

references.title: Appendix B to Part 30: Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards
references.note: OCC version of the same guidelines for national banks and federal savings associations.

references.title: Computer-Security Incident Notification Requirements for Banking Organizations and Their Bank Service Providers (86 FR 66424)
references.provision: 12 CFR 53.2-53.4 (OCC); 12 CFR 225 Subpart N (Board); 12 CFR Part 304 (FDIC)
references.note: Banking organizations notify their primary federal regulator as soon as possible and no later than 36 hours after determining a notification incident has occurred; bank service providers notify affected bank customers as soon as possible of incidents disrupting covered services for four or more hours.

references.title: Cybersecurity Regulation 23 NYCRR Part 500
references.note: Covered entities need a risk-based program, a CISO and board oversight, access limits and MFA, third-party policies, at least annual awareness training that includes social engineering, tested incident plans, notice to DFS within 72 hours of determining a cybersecurity incident and an annual compliance filing by April 15.

references.title: Part 500 Requirement Checklist for DFS-Regulated Entities with 500.19(a) Limited Exemptions
references.note: DFS checklist for smaller entities; lists the duties that still apply under a limited exemption, including at least annual awareness training with social engineering for all staff.

references.title: Cybersecurity FAQs
references.note: Confirms that DFS-licensed New York branches, agencies and representative offices of foreign banks are covered entities, and that a covered entity must notify DFS of an incident at its third-party service provider even if the provider also notifies DFS.

references.title: Third-Party Relationships: Interagency Guidance on Risk Management (Bulletin 2023-17)
references.note: Joint guidance on the life cycle of third-party relationships: planning, due diligence, contracts, monitoring and termination.

references.title: SR 23-4: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management
references.note: Federal Reserve transmittal of the same interagency guidance.

references.title: Consent Order: Capital One, N.A. and Capital One Bank (USA), N.A. (AA-EC-20-51, civil money penalty)
references.note: 2020 enforcement action for noncompliance with the information security guidelines: weak risk assessment before a cloud migration, audit gaps and a board that did not hold management accountable; USD 80 million penalty.

references.title: Consent Order to PayPal, Inc.
references.note: 2025 Part 500 settlement: untrained engineers skipped a required risk review, exposing customer data, and MFA was optional; USD 2 million penalty.

bank.question: A bank holding company owns a national bank in Ohio and a state member bank chartered in New York. Which statement about their cybersecurity rulebooks is correct?
options: Both follow the Interagency Guidelines; only the New York bank must also meet Part 500
Neither follows the guidelines because the holding company has a group program
Only the New York bank must follow the Interagency Guidelines
Both must meet Part 500 because they share a holding company
bank.explanation: The Interagency Guidelines apply to banks supervised by the OCC, the Fed and the FDIC. Part 500 covers entities operating under New York licenses or charters, so it reaches the New York bank but not the Ohio national bank.

bank.question: An examiner asks Kestrel Point to show how it decided which security controls to adopt from the list in the federal guidelines, such as encryption and dual control. What does the guidelines' structure expect?
options: The regulator picks the measures for the bank at each exam
The bank must adopt every listed measure regardless of its size
The bank considers each listed measure and adopts those its risk assessment shows are appropriate
The bank may ignore the list if its board approves
bank.explanation: Paragraph III.C.1 tells each bank to consider whether each listed security measure is appropriate and adopt those it concludes are, designing controls to fit the sensitivity of information and the complexity of its activities.

bank.question: A New York branch of a foreign bank uses its parent's global security program. DFS examiners find the program has no yearly awareness training for branch staff. What follows?
options: The branch is compliant because the parent's home regulator approved the program
Only the parent can be cited, since it wrote the program
The branch is out of compliance, because an adopted program must still meet every applicable Part 500 section
Training is not required for branches of foreign banks
bank.explanation: Part 500.2(d) lets a covered entity adopt an affiliate's program only if the provisions satisfy Part 500. DFS states that licensed New York branches of foreign banks are covered entities, and yearly awareness training applies to all personnel.

bank.question: Which situation best matches a 'Class A company' under Part 500?
options: A covered entity with at least USD 20 million in revenue, counted as the rule sets out, in each of the last two years and over 2,000 group employees
Any covered entity with more than 20 employees
Any covered entity that is a member of the Federal Reserve
A covered entity that had a cybersecurity incident in the last two years
bank.explanation: Class A requires at least USD 20 million gross annual revenue in each of the last two fiscal years from the entity and its affiliates' New York operations, plus either over 2,000 employees averaged over two years or over USD 1 billion group revenue.

bank.question: A compliance officer says: 'Under the federal guidelines our board must approve a new security training course every year.' What is the most accurate correction?
options: Correct; each course needs a board resolution every year
The board approves and oversees the written program; the guidelines require staff training but set no yearly course approval
The OCC, not the board, approves training courses
Training is outside the federal guidelines altogether
bank.explanation: The board approves the written program, oversees it and receives a yearly report. Training staff is a risk control duty, but the guidelines prescribe no course, frequency or board approval of each course.

bank.question: Which pair of objectives is part of the federal information security program objectives?
options: Protect against anticipated threats, and ensure proper disposal of customer and consumer information
Protect trade secrets, and prevent insider trading
Detect money laundering, and file currency transaction reports
Maximise system uptime, and reduce IT costs
bank.explanation: The four objectives are: security and confidentiality of customer information; protection against anticipated threats; protection against unauthorized access or use that could cause substantial harm or inconvenience; and proper disposal.

bank.question: A small DFS-licensed lender qualifies for a limited exemption and decides to drop both its awareness training and its multi-factor authentication. What is wrong with this plan?
options: The exemption does not remove the awareness training, and MFA is still required at least for remote and privileged access
Nothing; the limited exemption removes all of Part 500
Only the training decision is wrong; MFA can be dropped entirely
Only the MFA decision is wrong; training can be dropped
bank.explanation: The limited exemption removes sections such as 500.4, 500.5 and 500.16 and parts of 500.14, but not 500.14(a)(3) training. Under 500.12(a), limited-exempt entities still need MFA for remote access, remote access to third-party apps with nonpublic information and privileged accounts.

bank.question: Which lesson about training does the 2025 PayPal settlement best illustrate?
options: Training is only a concern for customer-facing staff
Phishing simulations replace the need for policy training
Staff who change systems must be trained on the policies they are expected to follow, or the policies fail
A company with good policies cannot be cited for training gaps
bank.explanation: DFS found the engineering team was not adequately trained on deployment policies, skipped the required risk review and exposed full Social Security numbers. Good policies did not help because the people applying them were not trained.

bank.question: A covered entity gives its awareness training only to employees, not to the contractors who use its systems every day. Which Part 500 risk does this create?
options: The training duty covers all personnel, so leaving out contractors with system access is likely a gap
None, because Part 500 applies only to employees on payroll
Contractors are covered only if they are Class A companies
Contractors must be trained by DFS directly
bank.explanation: Section 500.14(a)(3) requires training for all personnel, and Part 500 counts contractors and agents who use the entity's systems as authorized users. Leaving them out of training is likely to be treated as a gap.

bank.question: A caller with a confident voice says he is a DFS examiner and needs a teller to email him a list of large customers' account numbers today 'to check the exam file'. What should the teller do?
options: Send the list, because regulators are entitled to bank data
Ask the caller for his badge number and then send it
Send the list but remove the customers' names
Decline, verify through the bank's compliance team using known contacts, and report the call
bank.explanation: Impersonating a regulator is a common pretext. Real examination requests go through the bank's designated contacts. A badge number given by the caller proves nothing; verification must use a channel the bank already trusts.

bank.question: Why did DFS's Twitter report recommend hardware security keys over app-based push approvals?
options: Hardware keys are cheaper than smartphones
Hardware keys remove the need for any training
Push approvals are banned by Part 500
Hardware keys resist the trick of getting staff to approve a login started on a fake page
bank.explanation: In the Twitter hack, staff entered credentials on a look-alike page and approved push prompts. DFS noted that hardware MFA would have stopped the attackers, while still recommending training.

bank.question: Kestrel Point's risk assessment shows that most fraud attempts against staff now arrive by phone, not email, yet the yearly course covers only email phishing. Which change best meets Part 500?
options: Update the course to cover phone-based social engineering identified in the risk assessment
Move the topic to the IT team's technical training only
Ask DFS to approve the existing course as sufficient
Keep the course and add a second email phishing test
bank.explanation: Part 500 requires awareness training that includes social engineering and is updated to reflect risks the entity identifies in its risk assessment. Phone attacks are social engineering and should be covered for all personnel.

bank.question: An executive assistant gets an email from the CEO's account, which a phishing attack has really taken over, asking her to buy gift cards for a client event and send the codes. What is the best protection?
options: A rule to verify unusual payment or gift requests in person or by a known phone number, even from real accounts
Checking that the sender address exactly matches the CEO's
Waiting for the CEO to send a second email to confirm
Buying the cards but only sending half the codes
bank.explanation: When an account is genuinely compromised, the sender address is real, so address checks fail. Out-of-band verification through a known channel is what stops business email compromise.

bank.question: Which training content does the Fed's compliance guide to the federal guidelines give as an example?
options: Training staff to write the bank's encryption software
Training staff to file yearly certifications with DFS
Training customers to set up multi-factor authentication
Training staff to recognise and respond to fraud schemes such as pretext calling
bank.explanation: The guide says institutions should, for example, train staff to recognise and respond to fraud and identity theft schemes such as pretext calling, give IT staff computer security training and train staff in proper disposal.

bank.question: An employee realises she approved an MFA prompt by mistake twenty minutes ago. She is embarrassed. What message should the bank's training culture give her?
options: Ask a colleague to log in from her machine to check
Change her password next week during the routine reset
Say nothing unless something visibly goes wrong
Report it now; fast reporting lets security end the session and reset access
bank.explanation: A mistaken approval may have let an attacker in. The Residential Mortgage case shows the harm of slow reporting and weak follow-up. Training should reward fast reporting so containment can start at once.

bank.question: A bank wants to know whether its awareness training is working. Which measure gives the best evidence?
options: The number of slides in the training deck
The percentage of staff who say they enjoyed the course
The cost of the training vendor's contract
Trends in phishing test click rates and reporting rates, plus real incident reports from staff
bank.explanation: Effectiveness shows in behaviour: fewer clicks and more reports in tests and real attacks. Completion records prove the duty was met, but behaviour measures show whether training changes risk.

bank.question: During the yearly access review, a manager approves all 40 of her team's access rights in two minutes without checking them. Which risk does this create?
options: The bank becomes a Class A company
The review breaches the 72-hour rule
No risk, because the review was completed on time
Excess access stays in place, so the review fails its purpose even though it is recorded
bank.explanation: Part 500 requires reviewing access and removing what is no longer needed. A rubber-stamp review produces a record without removing excess rights, which examiners treat as a weak control.

bank.question: A Class A company finds that blocking commonly used passwords is infeasible on one older platform. What does Part 500 allow?
options: The CISO may approve in writing, at least yearly, the infeasibility and equivalent or stronger compensating controls
DFS must be asked for a waiver before the platform is used
The platform may run without controls until replaced
The help desk may approve an exception for one year
bank.explanation: Section 500.7(c)(2) lets the CISO approve in writing, at least annually, the infeasibility of blocking common passwords and the use of reasonably equivalent or more secure compensating controls.

bank.question: Which control from the federal guidelines' list most directly addresses an employee handing customer data to someone who phones pretending to be the customer?
options: Procedures for system modifications
Encryption of backup tapes in storage
Environmental controls against fire and water damage
Access controls that prevent employees from giving customer information to people seeking it by fraud
bank.explanation: Paragraph III.C.1.a includes controls to prevent employees from providing customer information to unauthorized individuals who may seek it through fraudulent means, which is the pretext scenario.

bank.question: Under Part 500, which group of users must use multi-factor authentication at a covered entity that does NOT have a limited exemption?
options: Only administrators
Only customers using online banking
Any individual accessing any of the covered entity's information systems
Only remote users
bank.explanation: After the 2023 amendment, 500.12(a) requires MFA for any individual accessing any information systems of a covered entity, unless it has a limited exemption, in which case a narrower set applies.

bank.question: A teller at a New York-chartered bank wants a colleague to use her login while she is on leave 'so customers aren't kept waiting'. What is the core problem?
options: It is fine as long as the password is changed afterwards
It is only a problem if the colleague makes an error
It is allowed if the branch manager agrees verbally
Shared credentials break accountability and the access limits the bank must keep
bank.explanation: Access must be limited to what each user's job requires, and actions must be traceable to a person. DFS cited shared admin accounts at OneMain because they hide who did what.

bank.question: Which pair correctly matches Part 500 encryption duties?
options: In transit only within the internal network
At rest only, with no alternative allowed
In transit over external networks and at rest, with CISO-approved alternatives if at-rest encryption is infeasible
Only for data sent to DFS or the Federal Reserve
bank.explanation: Section 500.15 requires a written policy for encryption meeting industry standards in transit over external networks and at rest, with CISO-approved compensating controls where at-rest encryption is infeasible, reviewed at least yearly.

bank.question: A bank is shredding old loan files. Which rulebook expects proper disposal of customer information?
options: Neither; disposal is only a matter of internal policy
Only Part 500, since it is the stricter rule
Both: the federal guidelines include disposal, and Part 500 requires secure disposal of nonpublic information no longer needed
Only the federal guidelines, since Part 500 covers electronic data only
bank.explanation: The federal guidelines make proper disposal an objective and a control, and Part 500.13(b) requires policies for secure disposal of certain nonpublic information no longer necessary, unless law requires retention.

bank.question: Kestrel Point has a written policy requiring MFA for remote access, but the setting was never switched on for one vendor portal that holds customer data. Which case shows how DFS views this?
options: Capital One 2020, where DFS fined a national bank
Residential Mortgage 2021, where the firm had no MFA at all
PayPal 2025, where a policy required strong authentication but MFA was optional in practice
Twitter 2020, where hackers used malware
bank.explanation: DFS cited PayPal for failing to use effective controls although its policy called for risk-based authentication. Capital One was an OCC action, and Residential Mortgage did have MFA.

bank.question: Kestrel Point's core platform is hit by ransomware on Monday at 9 am. At 1 pm the CISO determines that branches cannot serve customers and that it is a notification incident. By when must the Fed hear about it?
options: No later than 9 pm on Tuesday
No later than 1 pm on Thursday
Within 36 business hours of 9 am Monday
As soon as possible and no later than 1 am on Wednesday
bank.explanation: The 36 hours run from the determination that a notification incident has occurred, here 1 pm Monday, so the outside limit is 1 am Wednesday. The rule also says as soon as possible, so earlier is expected where possible.

bank.question: In the same incident, when does Kestrel Point's latest deadline for the DFS notice fall, if the incident was determined at 1 pm Monday?
options: 9 pm on Tuesday
1 pm on Thursday
1 am on Wednesday
The following Monday
bank.explanation: Part 500.17(a) requires notice as promptly as possible and no later than 72 hours after determining a cybersecurity incident. Seventy-two hours after 1 pm Monday is 1 pm Thursday.

bank.question: A cloud provider tells a national bank it will take its systems offline for a four-hour scheduled upgrade next Sunday, as agreed. Does the provider owe a notice under the federal incident rule when the upgrade happens?
options: Yes, because the outage lasts four hours
No; previously communicated scheduled maintenance is excluded
No, because cloud providers are never bank service providers
Yes, it must notify the OCC directly
bank.explanation: The bank service provider duty does not apply to scheduled maintenance, testing or software updates previously communicated to the bank customer.

bank.question: A bank service provider suffers an incident affecting a bank that never gave it a designated contact. Whom must the provider notify under the federal rule?
options: The bank's CEO and CIO, or two people with comparable responsibilities
Every customer of the bank
The bank's primary federal regulator
The bank's external auditor
bank.explanation: If no bank-designated point of contact was provided, the rule requires notice to the bank's CEO and CIO, or two individuals of comparable responsibility, through any reasonable means.

bank.question: Staff at a covered entity report 300 phishing emails in a week; none succeeded. Must the entity give DFS a 72-hour incident notice?
options: Yes, every cybersecurity event must be reported within 72 hours
Yes, if more than 100 emails were received
No, because phishing is outside Part 500
Generally no; unsuccessful attempts are cybersecurity events, not incidents, unless a notice trigger applies
bank.explanation: A cybersecurity event includes unsuccessful attempts, but the 72-hour notice applies to cybersecurity incidents: events needing notice to a government body, likely to cause material harm, or deploying ransomware. DFS encourages voluntary sharing of notable attempts.

bank.question: A bank discovers that an intruder accessed a file containing customers' names and account numbers. Under the federal response program guidance, what should it do about its primary federal regulator?
options: Notify it only after customers have been told
Notify it only if the 36-hour rule's disruption test is met
Notify it promptly once aware of unauthorized access to sensitive customer information
Never; customer data incidents go only to FinCEN
bank.explanation: The response program guidance expects prompt notice to the primary federal regulator once the bank becomes aware of unauthorized access to sensitive customer information, separate from the 36-hour rule's disruption-based test.

bank.question: Which element must a Part 500 incident response plan include?
options: A commitment never to restore from backups
A rule that only the board may declare an incident
Preparation of a root cause analysis describing how the event happened, its impact and how to prevent recurrence
A list of approved ransom payment brokers
bank.explanation: Section 500.16(a)(1) lists plan areas including goals, internal processes, roles and decision authority, communications, remediation, documentation, recovery from backups, root cause analysis and plan updates.

bank.question: A covered entity paid an extortion demand on Tuesday at 10 am. What is the latest time for its notice of payment to DFS?
options: Within 30 days
Wednesday at 10 am
Friday at 10 am
Only when the written explanation is ready
bank.explanation: Section 500.17(c) requires notice within 24 hours of the extortion payment, then a written explanation of reasons, alternatives and diligence, including OFAC compliance, within 30 days.

bank.question: After an incident, a bank notified its regulators within the deadlines. Two days later it learns that far more customer records were taken than first thought. What does Part 500 require?
options: Nothing, because the notice was already filed on time
Update DFS with the material new information
Withdraw the first notice and start a new 72-hour clock
Inform only the customers, not DFS
bank.explanation: Part 500.17(a)(2) gives covered entities a continuing obligation to update the Superintendent with material changes or new information that was previously unavailable.

bank.question: Under the federal guidelines, when must a bank monitor a service provider to confirm it is meeting its contractual security obligations?
options: Every month for every provider, whatever the risk
Where the bank's risk assessment indicates, for example by reviewing audits or test summaries
Never, because the contract transfers the risk
Only when the provider has a breach
bank.explanation: Paragraph III.D.3 requires monitoring where indicated by the bank's risk assessment, and says the bank should review audits, test result summaries or equivalent evaluations as part of it.

bank.question: A covered entity's CISO is employed by a managed security firm. Which statement fits Part 500?
options: Not allowed; the CISO must be on the entity's own payroll
Allowed only for Class A companies
Allowed, but the entity keeps responsibility, names a senior overseer and requires the firm to protect it under Part 500
Allowed, and responsibility for compliance passes to the firm
bank.explanation: Section 500.4(a) allows a CISO employed by an affiliate or third-party provider, provided the entity retains responsibility, designates a senior person to direct and oversee the provider, and requires the provider to maintain a compliant program.

bank.question: A board member says she does not understand cybersecurity reports and leaves them to management. Which Part 500 duty is at risk?
options: The duty to run penetration tests
The senior governing body must have sufficient understanding to oversee cybersecurity, using advisors if needed
The yearly 72-hour notice
The duty to encrypt data at rest
bank.explanation: Section 500.4(d)(1) requires the senior governing body to have sufficient understanding of cybersecurity matters to exercise oversight, which may include using advisors. Leaving reports unread undermines oversight.

bank.question: Which topic does the federal guidelines' yearly report to the board specifically suggest including?
options: Security breaches or violations and management's responses
Each employee's training score
The CISO's salary
The bank's lending targets
bank.explanation: Paragraph III.F says the report should discuss material matters such as the risk assessment, risk decisions, service provider arrangements, test results, security breaches or violations and management's responses, and recommended changes.

bank.question: Kestrel Point is merging with a smaller bank and moving both onto one cloud platform. Which federal guideline duty applies most directly?
options: Adjust the information security program for changes such as mergers and new systems, after assessing risk
Notify the Fed under the 36-hour rule before the migration
Only the acquired bank's program needs review
None, until the merger has closed for a full year
bank.explanation: Paragraph III.E requires the bank to monitor, evaluate and adjust its program for changes in technology, threats and business arrangements, including mergers and outsourcing. Capital One shows the cost of skipping risk assessment before a cloud move.

bank.question: Which evidence would best show DFS that the awareness training duty was met for last year?
options: A record that the board approved the training budget
Per-person completion records for all personnel, and course content updated for risks in the risk assessment
An email from the CISO saying training happened
A training vendor's brochure
bank.explanation: Part 500 requires training for all personnel, at least yearly, including social engineering and updated for identified risks. Completion records and updated content show both coverage and relevance, and support the April 15 filing.

bank.question: In setting a Part 500 penalty, which factor does DFS expressly consider?
options: Whether the CISO holds a particular certification
The extent to which the entity's policies are consistent with nationally recognised frameworks such as NIST
The entity's share price on the day of the incident
The number of social media followers the entity has
bank.explanation: Section 500.20(c) lists penalty factors including cooperation, good faith, intent, prior violations, harm to consumers, the board's participation and consistency with nationally recognised frameworks such as NIST.

bank.question: Under Part 500, what must a covered entity's yearly CISO report to the senior governing body cover?
options: Only the budget for next year
Material cybersecurity risks, the program's overall effectiveness, material events and plans to fix material gaps
Only the number of phishing emails blocked
Only incidents reported to DFS within 72 hours
bank.explanation: Section 500.4(b) requires a written report at least yearly covering, as applicable, confidentiality and integrity, policies, material risks, overall effectiveness, material events and remediation plans for material inadequacies.

bank.question: Which statement best sums up how the federal and New York layers fit together for a New York-chartered state member bank?
options: The federal guidelines replace Part 500 for any Fed member bank
It must meet the federal guidelines and 36-hour rule and also Part 500's more detailed duties, including yearly training and the 72-hour notice
Part 500 replaces the federal guidelines for any New York bank
It may choose whichever layer it prefers each year
bank.explanation: Neither layer displaces the other. A New York-chartered Fed member bank is supervised by the Fed under the federal rules and is also a DFS covered entity under Part 500, so it must satisfy both.
